title: Chai Discovery raises $400M Series C at $3.8B to scale AI molecular-design models used by Lilly, Novartis and Pfizer
subtitle: Two-year-old San Francisco startup triples its valuation in seven months as its Chai-3 model becomes an infrastructure layer for pharma drug discovery.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Chai Discovery raised $400 million in Series C financing on August 10 at a $3.8 billion valuation — nearly triple the $1.3B mark set seven months ago. Index Ventures led, with Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia and Dimension participating, plus new investors Bain Capital Ventures, Battery Ventures, Baillie Gifford, BDT & MSD, Sapphire Ventures and Avra Capital. Existing backers Thrive, OpenAI, Menlo, General Catalyst, Oak HC/FT, Avenir and Lachy Groom re-upped. Founded in 2024, Chai launched Chai-1 in its first year, shipped Chai-2 in August 2025, closed a $130M Series B in December, and unveiled Chai-3 this year alongside deals with Eli Lilly, Pfizer and Novartis.

The reason this round happened at that valuation is that Chai has quietly become an infrastructure layer for the top ranks of pharma. Chai's models predict how molecules will interact — protein-ligand binding, protein-protein interfaces, conformational change — and reprogram those interactions to hit a target. That work used to require months of wet-lab iteration per candidate; Chai-3 lets a medicinal chemist test hypotheses in silico first, ship only the promising ones to the bench, and cut the cycle time. Three top-ten pharma customers is not a pilot pattern — it is a bet that this becomes standard tooling.

This round arrives in a stretch when AI-designed drugs are finally reaching late-stage trials. Insilico Medicine's rentosertib is in Phase III, DeepHealth's ultrasound tool got FDA clearance in early August, and the Retina4iRD platform published in Nature Medicine last month. The pattern is that computational design isn't replacing biology — it is compressing the front end of drug discovery from years to quarters, and the companies that own the model layer capture recurring revenue from every large pharma that adopts them. Chai is now clearly one of those companies.

For learners interested in health AI: the interesting job is no longer 'train a bigger model.' It is at the interface of molecular biology and machine learning — how you represent a protein, how you encode a binding pocket, how you turn wet-lab data into a training signal. Anyone with a chemistry, biophysics or structural-biology background who picks up modern ML has a genuinely rare skill stack right now, and Chai's hiring pattern (biologists learning PyTorch, not the other way around) says exactly where the industry is investing.
